IndicatorDescription: Children tested for lead before age 3. In New York State, all children must be tested for lead before age 3. There is no safe level of lead in the blood.

Measures.how_calculated: Number of children born in New York City to New York City resident mothers tested for lead poisoning before the age of three years. To identify children tested for lead poisoning, birth records for all children born in a given year in New York City to New York City resident mothers were matched to children tested for lead poisoning in the New York City Childhood Lead Registry.
Measures.Sources: New York City Bureau of Vital Statistics; New York City Healthy Homes Program

Measures.how_calculated: Number of children born in New York City to New York City resident mothers who were tested for lead poisoning before the age of three years, divided by the number of children born in New York City to New York City resident mothers turning three years old; expressed as percent.
Measures.Sources: New York City Bureau of Vital Statistics; New York City Healthy Homes Program

IndicatorDescription: The risk of community-level heat impacts like deaths due to extreme heat events. The HVI is made from data on surface temperature, green space, air conditioning access, median income, and Black population (the population most excluded from heat resources). Differences in community-level heat impacts stem from structural racism, which limits access to preventive resources.

Measures.how_calculated: Each neighborhood receives a score from 1 (lowest risk) to 5 (highest risk) based on a statistical model that uses social and environmental factors to estimate risk of heat-related death across NYC neighborhoods. A low vulnerability score does not mean no risk. Every neighborhood has residents at risk for heat illness and death. Residents who are at highest heat risk are those who do not have or use air conditioning and are older or have chronic health conditions or serious mental illnesses.
Measures.Sources: American Community Survey 5 year estimates, 2016-2020; LiDAR, 2017, NYC Office of Information Technology; US Census, 2020; ECOSSTRESS thermal imaging, August 27, 2020, NASA; United States Census Housing and Vacancy Survey, 2017

IndicatorDescription: Concentration of TTHM in drinking water. Disinfection by-products form when a disinfectant such as chlorine reacts with naturally occurring organic matter in the source water. Current research is investigating whether there are health effects from chronic exposure to the by-products of water disinfection.

Measures.MeasureName: Disinfection by-products (TTHM), Qtr maximum allowable contaminant level (MCL)
Measures.how_calculated: The highest level of TTHM that is allowed in drinking water according to regulatory standards
Measures.Sources: United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)

Measures.how_calculated: Samples are collected from the drinking water distribution system, and concentrations of chloroform, bromodichloromethane, dibromochloromethane, and bromoform are summed within samples to derive a measure of total trihalomethane (TTHM). If a concentration is below the limit of detection (LOD), a value equal to one half the LOD is assigned. Total concentrations are averaged over each quarter.
Measures.Sources: New York State Safe Drinking Water Information System

Measures.how_calculated: Samples are collected from the drinking water distribution system, and concentrations of chloroform, bromodichloromethane, dibromochloromethane, and bromoform are summed within samples to derive a measure of total trihalomethane (TTHM). If a concentration is below the limit of detection (LOD), a value equal to one half the LOD is assigned. The maximum total concentration is identified for each quarter.
Measures.Sources: New York State Safe Drinking Water Information System

Measures.MeasureName: Disinfection by-products (TTHM), Maximum allowable contaminant level (MCL)
Measures.how_calculated: The highest level of total trihalomethanes (TTHM) that is allowed in drinking water according to regulatory standards.
Measures.Sources: United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)

Measures.how_calculated: Samples are collected from the drinking water distribution system, and concentrations of chloroform, bromodichloromethane, dibromochloromethane, and bromoform are summed within samples to derive a measure of total trihalomethane (TTHM). If a concentration is below the limit of detection (LOD), a value equal to one half the LOD is assigned. The maximum total concentration is identified for each year.
Measures.Sources: New York State Safe Drinking Water Information System

Measures.how_calculated: The number of total trihalomethanes (TTHM) samples taken throughout the distribution system.
Measures.Sources: New York State Safe Drinking Water Information System

Measures.how_calculated: Samples are collected from the drinking water distribution system, and concentrations of chloroform, bromodichloromethane, dibromochloromethane, and bromoform are summed within samples to derive a measure of total trihalomethane (TTHM). If a concentration is below the limit of detection (LOD), a value equal to one half the LOD is assigned. Total concentrations are averaged over the year.
Measures.Sources: New York State Safe Drinking Water Information System

Measures.how_calculated: The number of total trihalomethanes (TTHM) samples taken throughout the distribution system.
Measures.Sources: New York State Safe Drinking Water Information System

IndicatorDescription: Hospitalizations for asbestosis. Asbestos is a naturally-occurring mineral which was commonly used as an insulation material until the 1970s. Inhaling asbestos fibers can result in the chronic lung disease called asbestosis, a type of pneumoconiosis. New York City construction, insulation, and shipyard workers who installed, disturbed, or removed asbestos without respiratory protection are at risk. Typically it takes more than ten years before symptoms develop. The use of proper protective masks is key to preventing the disease, since there is no treatment.

Measures.how_calculated: Number of hospitalizations with an asbestosis ICD-9-CM diagnosis code of 501, among NYC residents aged 15 years or older, over a three-year period, divided by the population of NYC residents aged 15 years or older, expressed as 3-year Average annual rate per 100,000 residents.
Measures.Sources: Statewide Planning and Research Cooperative System; U.S. Census Bureau Population Estimates (V2016)

Measures.how_calculated: Number of hospitalizations with an asbestosis ICD-9-CM diagnosis code of 501, among NYC residents aged 15 years or older, over a 3-year period.
Measures.Sources: Statewide Planning and Research Cooperative System

IndicatorDescription: Blood lead levels over 10 mg/dL among people age 16+. In New York City, the most common cause of lead poisoning in non-pregnant adults is from working in the construction. Workers are exposed through lead dust or fumes during work that disturbs old lead paint. Workers in other industries, as well as hobbyists, may be at risk if they work with lead-containing metal, paint, pigments, ceramic glazes or bullets. Adults can also be exposed to lead through lead-contaminated products, like some imported health remedies, spices, foods, pottery and cosmetics.

Measures.MeasureName: Elevated blood lead levels (age 16+), Number (10+ mcg/dL)
Measures.how_calculated: Number of NYC residents aged 16 years or older with blood lead levels (BLL) greater than or equal to 10 micrograms per deciliter over the 3-year period.
Measures.Sources: New York State Heavy Metal Registry

Measures.MeasureName: Elevated blood lead levels (age 16+), Average annual rate (25+ mcg/dL)
Measures.how_calculated: Number of NYC residents aged 16 years and older with blood lead levels greater than or equal to 25 micrograms per deciliter over the 3-year period, divided by the employed NYC population aged 16 years or older in each of the 3 years, expressed as 3-year Average annual rate per 100,000 employed persons.
Measures.Sources: New York State Heavy Metal Registry; U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey

Measures.MeasureName: Elevated blood lead levels (age 16+), Number (25+ mcg/dL)
Measures.how_calculated: Number of NYC residents aged 16 years or older with blood lead levels greater than or equal to 25 micrograms per deciliter over the 3-year period.
Measures.Sources: New York State Heavy Metal Registry

Measures.MeasureName: Elevated blood lead levels (age 16+), Average annual rate (10+ mcg/dL)
Measures.how_calculated: Number of NYC residents aged 16 years and older with blood lead levels greater than or equal to 10 micrograms per deciliter over the 3-year period, divided by the employed NYC population aged 16 years or older in each of the 3 years, expressed as 3-year Average annual rate per 100,000 employed persons.
Measures.Sources: New York State Heavy Metal Registry; U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey

IndicatorDescription: Hospitalizations for pneumoconiosis, a lung disease caused by breathing in certain particles or fibers over a prolonged period. Pneumoconiosis usually results from a workplace exposure. The most common causes of pneumoconiosis include asbestos fibers, silica dust, and coal dust. There is no cure, but it can be prevented with appropriate respiratory protection.

Measures.how_calculated: Number of hospitalizations with a pneumoconiosis ICD-9-CM diagnosis code 500 - 505 or an ICD-10-CM diagnosis code J60 - J64, among NYC residents aged 15 years or older, divided by the population of NYC residents aged 15 years or older, expressed as 3-year Average annual rate per 100,000 residents.
Measures.Sources: Statewide Planning and Research Cooperative System; U.S. Census Bureau Population Estimates (V2016)

Measures.how_calculated: Number of hospitalizations with a pneumoconiosis ICD-9-CM diagnosis code 500 - 505 or an ICD-10-CM diagnosis code J60 - J64, among NYC residents aged 15 years or older, over a 3-year period.
Measures.Sources: Statewide Planning and Research Cooperative System

IndicatorDescription: Hospitalizations billed to workers' compensation. Workers' compensation provides medical care for workers injured or become ill as a direct result of their job. Hospitalizations billed to workers' comp represent only a portion of work-related injuries that require hospital care. Workers' compensation policies vary from state-to-state.

Measures.MeasureName: Hospitalizations billed to workers' compensation, Average annual rate
Measures.how_calculated: Number of hospitalizations among employed NYC residents aged 16 years or older with workers' compensation listed as the primary payer over a 3-year period, divided by the population of employed NYC residents aged 16 years or older in each of these years, expressed as a 3-year Average annual rate per 100,000.
Measures.Sources: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey; Statewide Planning and Research Cooperative System

Measures.MeasureName: Hospitalizations billed to workers' compensation, Number (employed)
Measures.how_calculated: Number of hospitalizations among employed NYC residents aged 16 years or older with workers' compensation listed as the primary payer in hospital discharge data over a 3-year period.
Measures.Sources: Statewide Planning and Research Cooperative System

IndicatorDescription: Fatal, work-related injuries. These include deaths resulting from unintentional injuries such as falls, acute poisonings, and motor vehicle crashes that occur during travel for work, and intentional injuries (i.e., homicides and suicides) that occur at work.

Measures.how_calculated: Number of fatal work-related injuries occurring in NYC and reported to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries. CFOI produces statistics on fatal work-related injuries by cross-referencing multiple sources, such as death certificates, workers' compensation reports, and Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) investigation reports.
Measures.Sources: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries

Measures.MeasureName: Work-related deaths (all industries), Estimated annual rate
Measures.how_calculated: Number of fatal work-related injuries occurring in NYC and reported to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, divided by the size of the NYC workforce, expressed as deaths per 10,000 workers.
Measures.Sources: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries; U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey

IndicatorDescription: Construction is the most dangerous industry in NYC, with nearly a third of work-related injury deaths each year. Falls from scaffolds, ladders and roofs are the most common cause of fatal injuries among construction workers.

Measures.how_calculated: Number of fatal construction injuries occurring in NYC and reported to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries.
Measures.Sources: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries

Measures.MeasureName: Work-related deaths (construction industry), Citywide, Annual rate
Measures.how_calculated: Number of fatal construction injuries occurring in NYC and reported to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, divided by the NYC construction workforce, expressed as deaths per 10,000 workers.
Measures.Sources: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries; U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey

IndicatorName: Elevated blood lead levels (under age 6), by NTA
IndicatorLabel: Elevated blood lead levels (under age 6), by NTA
IndicatorDescription: Elevated blood lead levels are 5+ mcg/dL. There is no safe level of lead in the blood. Lead poisoning can cause learning and behavior problems, and delay growth and mental development.

Measures.MeasureName: Child lead poisoning, by NTA, Average annual number (5+ mcg/dL)
Measures.how_calculated:
Sum of the number of children under 6 years of age with blood lead levels (BLL) 5 mcg/dL or greater over the time period, divided by the number of years in the time period. While children can receive more than one test during the calendar year, for this measure children are only counted once per year using the highest confirmed blood lead level during the calendar year. If the child does not have a confirmed test in a given year, the child’s blood lead level is based on the highest capillary or unknown test type. Read more about different measures used by the Health Department for surveillance of childhood lead poisoning.

  • For the purpose of providing data for small geographic areas, multiple years of data were combined to get sufficient numbers of observations to make more reliable estimates for a greater number of neighborhood tabulation areas (NTAs).
  • Annual numbers and rates of children under 6 years of age with elevated blood lead levels at the citywide, borough, and United Hospital Fund neighborhood level are available here.
Measures.Sources: New York City Healthy Homes Program

Measures.MeasureName: Child lead poisoning, by NTA, Average annual number tested
Measures.how_calculated: Average annual number of children under 6 years of age tested for lead poisoning. Children may be tested multiple times in a given year but for this measure are only counted once per year. All children are counted regardless of blood specimen type (confirmed or unconfirmed). Numbers are rounded to nearest 10. Read more about definitions and measures used by the Health Department for surveillance of childhood lead poisoning.
Measures.Sources: New York City Healthy Homes Program

Measures.MeasureName: Child lead poisoning, by NTA, Rate (5+ mcg/dL)
Measures.how_calculated:
Number of children under 6 years of age tested with blood lead levels (BLL) 5 mcg/dL or greater, divided by the total number of children under 6 years of age who were tested; expressed as cases per 1,000 tested. While children can receive more than one test during the calendar year, for this measure children are only counted once per year using the highest confirmed blood lead level during the calendar year. If the child does not have a confirmed test in a given year, the child’s blood lead level is based on the highest capillary or unknown test type. Read more about different measures used by the Health Department for surveillance of childhood lead poisoning.

  • For the purpose of providing data for small geographic areas, multiple years of data were combined to get sufficient numbers of observations to make more reliable estimates for a greater number of neighborhood tabulation areas (NTAs). 
  • Annual numbers and rates of children under 6 years of age with elevated blood lead levels at the citywide, borough, and United Hospital Fund neighborhood level are available here.
Measures.Sources: New York City Healthy Homes Program

IndicatorDescription: Babesiosis is a rare, sometimes severe or fatal tick-borne disease caused by a parasite that infects red blood cells. Babesiosis is transmitted by the bite of an infected blacklegged tick (the same tick that transmits Lyme disease and anaplasmosis). Most patients acquire this disease while traveling outside NYC. However, there has been an increase in the number of cases with no history of travel to endemic areas, primarily in Staten Island, as well as isolated cases in the Bronx and Queens. Babesiosis can also be transmitted through transfused blood products.

Measures.how_calculated: Number of cases meeting the national case definition.
Measures.Sources: NYC DOHMH Bureau of Communicable Disease

Measures.how_calculated: Age-adjusted rates were calculated per 100,000 population using NYC DOHMH population estimates, modified from US Census Bureau interpolated intercensal estimates, updated April 2017.
Measures.Sources: NYC DOHMH Bureau of Communicable Disease

Measures.how_calculated: Crude Rate per 100,000 Population
Measures.Sources: NYC DOHMH Bureau of Communicable Disease

IndicatorDescription: Adults reporting that their health is excellent, very good, or good.

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of adults who report their overall health as "excellent," "very good" or "good" on a scale of one to five (excellent, very good, good, fair or poor), rounded to the nearest 1,000.
Measures.Sources: New York City Community Health Survey (CHS)

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of adults who report their overall health as "excellent," "very good" or "good" on a scale of one to five (excellent, very good, good, fair or poor), divided by all adults; expressed as percent.
Measures.Sources: New York City Community Health Survey (CHS)

IndicatorName: Adults reporting personal use of pesticides
IndicatorDescription: Adults reporting pesticide use in the home. This does not include pesticide applications by professional exterminators.

Measures.MeasureName: Personal pesticide use, Percent (Tempo or Chinese Chalk)
Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of adults who reported using any illegal methods of pesticide (Tempo or Chinese Chalk) inside of the home to control insects, among pesticide users in the past 12 months, divided by all adults in the area; expressed as percent.
Measures.Sources: New York City Community Health Survey (CHS)

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of adults who reported using any ineffective methods of pesticide (Sprays or Foggers) inside of the home to control insects, among pesticide users in the past 12 months, divided by all adults in the area; expressed as percent.
Measures.Sources: New York City Community Health Survey (CHS)

Measures.MeasureName: Personal pesticide use, Number (Safer methods only)
Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of adults who reported using only safe methods of pesticide (Bait, Gel, or Boric acid) inside of the home to control insects, among pesticide users in the past 12 months, rounded to the nearest 1,000.
Measures.Sources: New York City Community Health Survey (CHS)

Measures.MeasureName: Personal pesticide use, Percent (Safer methods only)
Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of adults who reported using only safe methods of pesticide (Bait, Gel, or Boric acid) inside of the home to control insects, among pesticide users in the past 12 months, divided by all adults in the area; expressed as percent.
Measures.Sources: New York City Community Health Survey (CHS)

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of adults who reported using any pesticide inside of the home to control insects in the past 12 months, rounded to the nearest 1,000.
Measures.Sources: New York City Community Health Survey (CHS)

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of adults who reported using any pesticide inside of the home to control insects in the past 12 months, divided by all adults in the area; expressed as percent.
Measures.Sources: New York City Community Health Survey (CHS); New York City Child Community Health Survey

IndicatorDescription: Adults reporting driving in the last 30 days (from when they were surveyed).

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of adults who reported driving in NYC in the last 30 days, rounded to the nearest 1,000.
Measures.Sources: New York City Community Health Survey (CHS)

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated percent of adults who reported driving in NYC in the last 30 days; expressed as a percent.
Measures.Sources: New York City Community Health Survey (CHS)

IndicatorDescription: Adults reporting messaging while driving in the past 30 days (from when they were surveyed).

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of adult drivers (drove in the last 30 days) who responded "often", "sometimes" or "rarely" to the question: "In the past 30 days, when you drove in New York City, how often have you read or sent a text message or email while you were driving?"
Measures.Sources: New York City Community Health Survey (CHS)

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated percent of adult drivers (drove in the last 30 days) who responded "often", "sometimes" or "rarely" to the question: "In the past 30 days, when you drove in New York City, how often have you read or sent a text message or email while you were driving?"
Measures.Sources: New York City Community Health Survey (CHS)

IndicatorDescription: Adults reporting speeding while driving in the past 30 days (from when they were surveyed).

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of adult drivers (drove in the last 30 days) who responded "often", "sometimes" or "rarely" to the question: "In the past 30 days, when you drove in New York City, how often did you drive 10 miles per hour or more over the posted speed limit?"
Measures.Sources: New York City Community Health Survey (CHS)

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated percent of adult drivers (drove in the last 30 days) who responded "often", "sometimes" or "rarely" to the question: "In the past 30 days, when you drove in New York City, how often did you drive 10 miles per hour or more over the posted speed limit?"
Measures.Sources: New York City Community Health Survey (CHS)

IndicatorDescription: Construction is the most dangerous industry in NYC, with nearly a third of work-related injury deaths each year.

Measures.MeasureName: Work-related deaths (construction industry), by borough, Number
Measures.how_calculated: Number of fatal construction injuries occurring in NYC by borough in which the injury occurred, across all 3 years.
Measures.Sources: New York City Bureau of Vital Statistics; NYC Office of Chief Medical Examiner; U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey

IndicatorDescription: Pest control services provided by a professional exterminator in the individual's home.

Measures.how_calculated: Sum of gallons (gal) of liquid pesticide applications that meet the following qualifications: classified as insect growth regulator, insecticide, miticide, mechanical, or termiticide.
Measures.Sources: New York State Pesticide Sales and Use Registry (PSUR)

Measures.how_calculated: Sum of pounds (lb) of solid pesticide applications that meet the following qualifications: classified as insect growth regulator, insecticide, miticide, "mechanical", or termiticide.
Measures.Sources: New York State Pesticide Sales and Use Registry (PSUR)

Measures.how_calculated: Sum of gallons (gal) of liquid pesticide applications that meet the following qualifications: classified as insect growth regulator, insecticide, miticide, or termiticide; and containing active ingredient of the chemical class N-methyl carbamate
Measures.Sources: New York State Pesticide Sales and Use Registry (PSUR)

Measures.how_calculated: Sum of pounds (lb) of solid pesticide applications that meet the following qualifications: classified as insect growth regulator, insecticide, miticide, or termiticide; and containing active ingredients of the chemical class N-methyl carbamate
Measures.Sources: New York State Pesticide Sales and Use Registry (PSUR)

Measures.how_calculated: Sum of gallons (gal) of liquid pesticide applications that meet the following qualifications: classified as insect growth regulator, insecticide, miticide, or termiticide; and containing active ingredient of the chemical class organophosphorous compound.
Measures.Sources: New York State Pesticide Sales and Use Registry (PSUR)

Measures.how_calculated: Sum of pounds (lb) of solid pesticide applications that meet the following qualifications: classified as insect growth regulator, insecticide, miticide, or termiticide; and containing active ingredient of the chemical class organophosphorous compound.
Measures.Sources: New York State Pesticide Sales and Use Registry (PSUR)

Measures.how_calculated: Sum of gallons (gal) of liquid pesticide applications that meet the following qualifications: classified as insect growth regulator, insecticide, miticide, or termiticide; and containing active ingredient of the chemical class pyrethrin or pyrethroid.
Measures.Sources: New York State Pesticide Sales and Use Registry (PSUR)

Measures.how_calculated: Sum of pounds (lb) of solid pesticide applications that meet the following qualifications: classified as insect growth regulator, insecticide, miticide, or termiticide; and containing active ingredient of the chemical class pyrethrin or pyrethroid.
Measures.Sources: New York State Pesticide Sales and Use Registry (PSUR)

Measures.MeasureName: Commercial insecticide use, Best practice products
Measures.how_calculated: Sum of pounds (lb) of solid pesticide applications that meet the following qualifications: classified as insect growth regulator, insecticide, miticide, or termiticide; having the term bait or gel in the product name, or containing active ingredients boric acid, disodium octaborate tetrahydrate, sodium tetraborate (pentahydrate), indoxacarb, silica gel, diatomaceous earth, (Z)-9-tricosene, S-methoprene, spinosad, hydramethylnon, pyriproxyfen, or fipronil; and not containing active ingredients of the chemical classes pyrethrins, pyrethroids, N-methyl carbamates or organophosphorous compounds.
Measures.Sources: New York State Pesticide Sales and Use Registry (PSUR)

IndicatorDescription: Adults incarcerated in NYC facilities. Each component of the criminal justice continuum - from arrest to re-entry - carries various health consequences, and a growing body of literature has documented severe adverse health outcomes for the individual, their families, and neighborhoods.

Measures.how_calculated: Crude rate of of incarcerated adults in NYC Department of Correction facilities per 1,000 population ages 18 and older. Addresses at admission to New York City Department of Correction facilities were geocoded; 69% of all records could be geocoded to a valid NTA. Data were limited to those ages 18 years of age and older and deduplicated by individuals' unique ID numbers and NTAs of residence. The six years of count data were annualized by dividing by six.
Measures.Sources: New York City Department of Correction

IndicatorDescription: Deaths before age 65. This can indicate the overall health of a population.

Measures.how_calculated: Average annual rate of premature deaths (death before age 65) per 100,000 population.
Measures.Sources: New York City Bureau of Vital Statistics; New York City Bureau of Vital Statistics; United States Census

Measures.how_calculated: Number of deaths occurring before age 65.
Measures.Sources: New York City Bureau of Vital Statistics

IndicatorDescription: Students missing 20 or more school days per year.

Measures.how_calculated: The percent of NYC public school students, grades K to 5, who were chronically absent during the 2013-14 school year. Chronically absent is defined as missing 20 or more school days per year.
Measures.Sources: New York City Department of Education

IndicatorDescription: Population by Census race/ethnicity category. Past and present structural racism has inequitably distributed resources that people need to stay healthy - like job opportunities, healthy housing, high-quality education, and health care.

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated percent of people who are only Asian.
Measures.Sources: American Community Survey

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated percent of people who are only Black.
Measures.Sources: American Community Survey

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated Percent Hispanic
Measures.Sources: American Community Survey

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated Percent White
Measures.Sources: American Community Survey

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated total population.
Measures.Sources: American Community Survey

Measures.how_calculated: Estiamted percent of people who are not White.
Measures.Sources: American Community Survey

IndicatorDescription: People age 25 years and over who have completed high school or high school equivalency.

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of people 25 years and over who have completed High School (Includes Equivalency).
Measures.Sources: American Community Survey

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of people 25 years and over who have completed High School (Includes Equivalency), divided by the total number of people 25 years and over; expressed as percent.
Measures.Sources: American Community Survey

IndicatorDescription: People who do not speak English at home and/or are not English proficient.

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of people who do not speak English at home and are not English Proficent.
Measures.Sources: American Community Survey

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of people who do not speak English at home and are not English Proficent, divided by the total population; expressed as percent.
Measures.Sources: American Community Survey

IndicatorDescription: Renter households spending 30% of their income or more on rent.

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of renter households whose gross rent (rent plus electricity and heating fuel costs) equals at least 30 percent of their income.
Measures.Sources: American Community Survey

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of renter households whose gross rent (rent plus electricity and heating fuel costs) equals at least 30 percent of their income, divided by the total number of households; expressed as percent.
Measures.Sources: American Community Survey

IndicatorDescription: Adults age 16+ who are unemployed.

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of people in the civilian labor force (16 years and older) who are unemployed. All civilians 16 years old and over are classified as unemployed if they (1) were neither "at work" nor "with a job but not at work" during the reference week, and (2) were looking for work during the last 4 weeks, and (3) were available to accept a job. Also included as unemployed are civilians who did not work at all during the reference week, were waiting to be called back to a job from which they had been laid off, and were available for work except for temporary illness.
Measures.Sources: American Community Survey

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of people in the civilian labor force (16 years and older) who are unemployed, divided by the total civilian labor force; expressed as percent.All civilians 16 years old and over are classified as unemployed if they (1) were neither "at work" nor "with a job but not at work" during the reference week, and (2) were looking for work during the last 4 weeks, and (3) were available to accept a job. Also included as unemployed are civilians who did not work at all during the reference week, were waiting to be called back to a job from which they had been laid off, and were available for work except for temporary illness.
Measures.Sources: American Community Survey

IndicatorName: Secondhand smoke at home (from outside sources)
IndicatorLabel: Secondhand smoke at home (from outside sources)
IndicatorDescription: Adults reporting secondhand smoke at home, from outside sources. Secondhand smoke, especially indoors, is bad for health - especially for the health of children.

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of people who reported smelling cigarette smoke everyday in their home that comes from another home or apartment or from the outside; expressed as percent.

IndicatorName: Youth with a recent asthma attack
IndicatorDescription: Public high school students who reported having an asthma attack in the past 12 months from when they were surveyed.

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of public high school students who reported having an asthma attack in the past 12 months, rounded to the nearest 1,000.
Measures.Sources: New York City Youth Risk Behavioral Survey

Measures.how_calculated: Estimated number of public high school students who reported having an asthma attack in the past 12 months, divided by the total number of public high school students; expressed as a percent.

IndicatorDescription: West Nile virus is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. IndicatorDescription: Non-fatal, violence-related injuries that result in hospitalizations. These are more common than homicides and help paint the larger picture of the burden of violence on communities.

Measures.how_calculated: Because of slight variations between datasets, results might differ from those calculated using a different extract. IndicatorDescription: The percentage of the population who live within walking distance to a park: a quarter-mile or less to entrances of smaller sites, such as sitting areas and playgrounds, and half-mile or less to entrances of larger parks. Increased access to green space and open space can contribute to increased levels of physical activity.

Measures.how_calculated: A map of "walk-to-a-park service areas" from the NYC Parks Department was overlayed onto a map of 2017 population estimates by census tract to calculate the percentage of the population that potentially live within the service area. These percentages were aggregated up to a neighborhood level.
Measures.Sources: New York City Department of Parks and Recreation; New York City DOHMH population estimates, modified from US Census Bureau inter-censal population estimates

IndicatorDescription: The ratio of bodegas to supermarkets. This can indicate whether the environment makes accessing unhealthy food easier for residents, as bodegas are less likely to have healthy food options than supermarkets.

Measures.how_calculated: The number of bodegas per supermarket within an area based on address of business. Bodegas are defined as food purchasing establishments with less than 4,000 square foot and excludes specialty stores, such as bakeries and vitamin stores. Supermarkets are defined as retail food purchasing establishments with greater than or equal to 10,000 square feet or have a chain supermarket name regardless of size.
Measures.Sources: NYS Department of Agriculture and Markets

IndicatorDescription: Percent of street milage with bike lanes. Bike lanes can improve bicyclist and pedestrian safety, physical activity, and sustainable transportation use.

Measures.how_calculated: Percentage of street mileage with conventional and protected bicycle lanes, not including sharrows, dirt trails, boardwalks, and velodromes.
Measures.Sources: New York City Department of Transportation

IndicatorName: Walking distance to a subway station
IndicatorDescription: The percentage of population within a quarter-mile of a subway station entrance. When more people have convenient access to the transit system, they're more likely to use it. Subway access encourages active transportation, which improves the health of residents.

Measures.how_calculated: Walking distance to a subway station is defined as 1/4-mile or less. Distance was measured between the centroid of 2010 Census blocks and the nearest station entrance. Census block populations within areas defined as walking distance were summed across the neighborhood and divided by total neighborhood population.
Measures.Sources: United States Census; Metropolitan Transportation Authority

Measures.how_calculated: The number of NYC residents treated in an emergency department (ED), including those admitted as inpatients after being seen in an ED. Prior to October 1, 2015*, includes those with an ICD-9-CM diagnosis code of 986 for carbon monoxide poisoning and any unintentional fire-related injury code within the range of E890.0-E899.9. Data from years prior to 2015 are not directly comparable to those after. IndicatorLabel: Home fall-related emergency department visits among older adults
IndicatorDescription: Emergency department visits due to home falls (age 65+). Falls are a leading cause of injury among older adults

Measures.how_calculated:
Because of slight variations between datasets, results might differ from those calculated using a different extract. Internal analyses by New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene conducted in March 2025. Age-adjusted rates were calculated from number of non-fatal fall-related injury emergency department visits divided by the corresponding age-specific NYC DOHMH population estimates, modified from US Census Bureau interpolated intercensal population estimates, 2000-2021 (updated September 2022) and 2020-2023 (updated March 2025). The resulting age-specific rates are multiplied by the proportion of the US Census 2000 population in each age group. Age-adjusted rate is the sum of these weighted rates, expressed as cases per 100,000 residents. Non-fatal fall-related injury emergency department visits were identified following the National Health Statistics Injury Framework for injury intent and mechanism classification using these first-listed external cause International Classification of Disease 10th Revision Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) codes: V00.11-V00.89 with 6th character=1; W00-W15, W17, W19; W16 with 6th character=2 (Except 16.4 and 16.9 with 5th character=2); W18.1, W18.2, W18.3 (National Center for Health Statistics). ED visits for a fall that occurred at home were identified using place of injury ICD10 code Y920 and then limited to the following building classes: "Condominiums", "Elevator Apartments", "One-family Dwellings", "Two-family Dwellings", "Walk-up Apartments", and "Residence Multiple Use". Only live discharges and initial encounters are included. All tables and figures include NYC residents only. Visits were restricted to patients ages 65+ years because of the disproportionate concentration of fall injury and its persistence as a high-ranking of cause of death in this age group.

Hospitalizations for a fall that occurred at home were identified using place of injury ICD-10-CM code Y920 and then limited to the following building classes: "Condominiums," "Elevator Apartments", "One-family Dwellings", "Two-family Dwellings", "Walk-up Apartments", and "Residence Multiple Use". Only live discharges and initial encounters are included. All tables and figures include NYC residents only. Visits were restricted to patients ages 65+ years because of the disproportionate concentration of fall injury and its persistence as a high-ranking of cause of death in this age group.

IndicatorDescription: Hospitalizations due to hot weather. These are part of the public health burden due to hot weather. Data aggregated over 10 years provides enough stablility to display neighborhood impacts.

Measures.MeasureName: Heat hospitalizations, Average annual age-adjusted rate
Measures.how_calculated: The number of NYC residents admitted to a NYC hospital during the months of May-September summed over a 10-year period for the effects of heat and light due to weather conditions or undetermined cause. Residents with a diagnosis of excessive heat due to non-environmental conditions were excluded. Data are based on date of admission and include those who were admitted with a diagnosis of heat-related illness, even if that was not the principal diagnosis. The data also include patients admitted to the hospital after being treated in an emergency department. Numbers are summed by 5-year age groups and divided by the population in each age group, using NYC DOHMH intercensal estimates. Quotients are multiplied by the proportion of the 2000 US population in each age group. The Average annual age-adjusted rate is the sum of the weighted age-specific rates; expressed as cases per 100,000 residents. Notes: The coding system used to represent diagnoses changed in October 2015. Cases admitted before October 1, 2015 are represented by International Classification of Diseases (ICD), 9th Edition, Clinical Modification (ICD-9-CM) codes 992.0-992.9, E900.0 or E900.9. Cases admitted on or after October 1, 2015, are represented by the ICD, 10th Edition, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) codes T67, X30, X32. Cases with diagnoses represented by ICD-9-CM code E900.1 (if admitted before October 1, 2015) or ICD-10-CM code W92 (if admitted on or after October 1, 2015) were excluded. Because of the October 1, 2015 change in diagnostic codes from ICD-9-CM to ICD-10-CM, changes in numbers and rates over time should be interpreted with caution because they may be in part due to changes in the coding system.
Measures.Sources: New York City DOHMH population estimates, modified from US Census Bureau inter-censal population estimates; Statewide Planning and Research Cooperative System

IndicatorDescription: The risk of community-level heat impacts, like deaths, due to extreme heat events. The HVI is made up of data on surface temperature, green space, air conditioning access, median income, and Black population (the population most excluded from heat resources). Differences in community-level heat impacts stem from structural racism, which limits access to preventive resources.

Measures.how_calculated: Each neighborhood receives a score from 1 (lowest risk) to 5 (highest risk) based on a statistical model that uses social and environmental factors to estimate risk of heat-related death across NYC neighborhoods. A low vulnerability score does not mean no risk. Every neighborhood has residents at risk for heat illness and death. Residents who are at highest heat risk are those who do not have or use air conditioning and are older or have chronic health conditions or serious mental illnesses.
Measures.Sources: American Community Survey 5 year estimates, 2016-2020; LiDAR, 2017, NYC Office of Information Technology; US Census, 2020; ECOSSTRESS thermal imaging, August 27, 2020, NASA; United States Census Housing and Vacancy Survey, 2017

IndicatorDescription: The average number of Citi Bikes available to rent per each area between 7am-7pm. Biking bridges gaps in existing public transportation systems and is a great way to exercise. Neighborhoods with lower Citi Bike availability have limited access to this beneficial public resource.

Measures.how_calculated: Yearly bike availability is calculated by totaling average daily bike availability and dividing by the number of days in the year. Average daily bike availability is calculated from totaling bikes available at every station per each area as reported at every hour mark from 7am to 7pm on a given day and dividing by the number of hours (13). Values are rounded to the nearest whole number after all calculations are complete.
Measures.Sources: Citi Bike GBFS feed

Average daily bike availability is calculated from totaling bikes available per 1000 people at every station per each area as reported at every hour mark from 7am to 7pm on a given day and dividing by the number of hours (13). Values are rounded to the single decimal place after all calculations are complete.
Measures.Sources: Citi Bike GBFS feed

IndicatorDescription: ED visits due to heat-related illnesses, such as heat stroke and heat exhaustion. These are part of the public health burden of extreme heat.

Measures.MeasureName: Heat stress: 5-year emergency department visits, Number
Measures.how_calculated: The number of NYC residents treated in a NYC emergency department (ED) over 5 years during the months of May-September for the effects of heat and light due to weather conditions or undetermined cause. Residents with a diagnosis of excessive heat due to non-environmental conditions were excluded. Data are based on date of visit and include those with a diagnosis of heat-related illness, even if that was not the principal diagnosis. The data also include patients admitted to the hospital after being treated in an emergency department. Notes: The coding system used to represent diagnoses changed in October 2015. Cases occuring before October 1, 2015 are represented by International Classification of Diseases (ICD), 9th Edition, Clinical Modification (ICD-9-CM) codes 992.0-992.9, E900.0 or E900.9. Cases admitted on or after October 1, 2015, are represented by the ICD, 10th Edition, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) codes T67, X30, X32. Cases with diagnoses represented by ICD-9-CM code E900.1 (if admitted before October 1, 2015) or ICD-10-CM code W92 (if admitted on or after October 1, 2015) were excluded. Because of the October 1, 2015 change in diagnostic codes from ICD-9-CM to ICD-10-CM, changes in numbers and rates over time should be interpreted with caution because they may be in part due to changes in the coding system.
Measures.Sources: New York State Statewide Planning and Research Cooperative System (SPARCS) Deidentified Hospital Discharge Data

Measures.MeasureName: Heat stress: 5-year emergency department visits, Average annual age-adjusted rate
Measures.how_calculated: The number of NYC residents treated in a NYC emergency department (ED) over 5 years during the months of May-September for the effects of heat and light due to weather conditions or undetermined cause. Annual data is based on date of admission, and include those who were treated in an ED with a diagnosis of cold-related illness in any principal or other diagnostic field. The data also include patients admitted to the hospital after being treated in an emergency department. Counts are summed by 5-year age groups and divided by the population in each age group, using NYC DOHMH intercensal estimates; quotients are multiplied by the proportion of the 2000 US population in each age group. Age-adjusted rate is the sum of the weighted age-specific rates; expressed as cases per 100,000 residents.

IndicatorDescription: Households reporting visible mold in the home. Mold can worsen respiratory conditions like asthma, and indicate maintenance problems in a building.

Measures.how_calculated:
Estimated number of households that reported visible mold in the home, divided by the number of households in the area; expressed as percent. Changes in survey methodology in 2021 may account for some of the differences with earlier time periods. More details available on NYC HPD's research page.

The Census Bureau has reviewed this data product for unauthorized disclosure of confidential information and has approved the disclosure limitation practices applied. (Disclosure Review Board (DRB) approval numbers: CBDRB-FY23-POP001-0073 and CBDRB FY24 0145)
Measures.Sources: New York City Housing and Vacancy Survey (NYCHVS)

IndicatorName: Homes with mice or rats in the unit or building
IndicatorLabel: Homes with mice or rats in the unit or building
IndicatorDescription: Households reporting mice or rats in their unit or building. The presence of mice or rats in the home is often associated with poor housing maintenance. These pests can contaminate food and worsen asthma.

Measures.MeasureName: Homes with mice or rats in the unit or building, Percent
Measures.how_calculated:
Estimated number of households that reported mice or rats in their unit or building in the past 90 days, divided by the number of households in the area; expressed as percent. Changes in survey methodology in 2021 may account for some of the differences with earlier time periods. More details available on NYC HPD's research page.

The Census Bureau has reviewed this data product for unauthorized disclosure of confidential information and has approved the disclosure limitation practices applied. (Disclosure Review Board (DRB) approval numbers: CBDRB-FY23-POP001-0073 and CBDRB FY24 0145)
Measures.Sources: New York City Housing and Vacancy Survey (NYCHVS)

IndicatorDescription: Concentration of fine particles in the air. Fine particles are emitted by vehicles, building boilers, and other combustion - and are a major form of air pollution that harms health. Regulatory PM2.5 sensors collect readings on the tops of buildings that measure regional changes in air quality for the federal Clean Air Act. This indicator is one of the federal standards for PM2.5 (9.0 µg/m3).

Measures.how_calculated: This measure is calculated by averaging PM2.5 levels at each monitor, weighted by the number of samples in each quarter, then taking the weighted average of all monitors in the geographic area.
Measures.Sources: United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Air Quality System (AQS) Data

Measures.how_calculated: 98% of PM2.5 measurements taken at New York City's EPA Air Quality Stations are below this value over the past three years. This value is one of the PM2.5 Federal Air Quality Standards. The standard is 65 mcg per cubic meter.
Measures.Sources: United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Air Quality System (AQS) Data
